title: Hansel and Gretel
paragraphs: Near a great forest lived a poor woodcutter with his wife and his two children. The boy was called Hansel and the girl Gretel. He had hardly anything to eat, and when a great famine struck the land, he couldn’t even get their daily bread any more. One night he lay in bed worrying about this, tossing and turning in his anxiety, and he groaned and said to his wife, “What is going to become of us? How can we feed our poor children, when we have nothing left even for ourselves?” “I’ll tell you what, husband,” the woman answered. “Early tomorrow morning we’ll take the children out into the forest, to the thickest part. We’ll light a fire for them there and give each of them one more piece of bread, and then we’ll go off to our work and leave them alone. They won’t find their way home again, and we’ll be rid of them.” “No, wife,” said the man, “I won’t do that. How could I bring myself to leave my children alone in the forest? The wild animals would soon come and tear them apart.” “Oh, you fool!” she said. “Then all four of us will starve to death, and you may as well start planing the boards for our coffins.” She gave him no peace until he agreed. “But I still feel sorry for the poor children,” said the man.

The two children hadn’t been able to sleep either, from hunger, and they had heard what their stepmother said to their father. Gretel wept bitter tears and said to Hansel, “It’s all over for us now.” “Hush, Gretel,” said Hansel. “Don’t upset yourself. I’ll find a way to help us.” When the old people had fallen asleep, he got up, put on his little coat, opened the door downstairs, and crept outside. The moon was shining brightly, and the white pebbles lying in front of the house glittered like silver coins. Hansel bent down and stuffed his coat pocket with as many as it would hold. Then he went back in and said to Gretel, “Take comfort, dear little sister, and sleep in peace. God won’t abandon us.” And he lay down in his bed again. At daybreak, before the sun had risen, the woman came and woke the two children. “Get up, you lazybones! We’re going into the forest to fetch wood.” She gave each of them a small piece of bread and said, “That’s for your midday meal, but don’t eat it before then, because you’ll get nothing else.” Gretel put the bread under her apron, since Hansel had the pebbles in his pocket. Then they all set out together for the forest. After they had walked a little way, Hansel stopped and looked back at the house, and he did this again and again. His father said, “Hansel, what are you staring at, and why do you keep lagging behind? Pay attention, and don’t forget how to use your legs.” “Oh, Father,” said Hansel, “I’m looking at my little white cat. She’s sitting up on the roof and wants to say goodbye to me.” The woman said, “Fool, that isn’t your cat. That’s the morning sun shining on the chimneys.” But Hansel hadn’t been looking at any cat. He had been taking one white pebble after another out of his pocket and dropping it on the road.

When they reached the middle of the forest, the father said, “Now, children, gather some wood, and I’ll make a fire so that you won’t be cold.” Hansel and Gretel collected brushwood and piled it as high as a small hill. The brushwood was lit, and when the flames were leaping high, the woman said, “Now, children, lie down by the fire and rest. We’re going into the forest to cut wood. When we’re finished, we’ll come back and get you.”

Hansel and Gretel sat by the fire, and at noon each of them ate a small piece of bread. Hearing the sound of an axe, they believed their father was close by. But it wasn’t an axe. It was a branch that he had tied to a dead tree, and the wind was swinging it back and forth. They had been sitting there so long that their eyes closed from tiredness, and they fell fast asleep. When they finally woke, it was already dark night. Gretel started to cry and said, “How are we ever going to get out of the forest?” But Hansel comforted her. “Just wait a little while, until the moon has risen, and then we’ll find the way easily.” And when the full moon had risen, Hansel took his little sister by the hand and followed the pebbles, which shone like freshly minted silver coins and showed them the way.

They walked all night long, and at daybreak they came back to their father’s house. They knocked at the door, and when the woman opened it and saw that it was Hansel and Gretel, she said, “You wicked children, why did you sleep so long in the forest? We thought you weren’t coming back at all!” The father, though, was overjoyed, because it had broken his heart to leave them behind alone.

Not long afterward there was great famine in the land once more, and the children heard their mother say to their father one night, “We’ve eaten everything again. We have half a loaf left, and then that’s the end. The children have to go. We’ll take them deeper into the woods, so they can’t find their way out again. There is no other way to save ourselves!” The man’s heart was heavy, and he thought, “It would be better to share our last mouthful with the children.” But the woman wouldn’t listen to anything he had to say. She scolded him and heaped reproaches on him. Whoever says A must say B too, and since he had given in the first time, he had to give in the second time as well.

But the children were still awake and had heard the conversation. When the old people were asleep, Hansel got up again and wanted to go out and gather pebbles as he had before. But the woman had locked the door, and Hansel couldn’t get out. Even so, he comforted his little sister and said, “Don’t cry, Gretel. Go to sleep quietly. The good God will help us.”

The woman came at dawn and pulled the children out of bed. They were handed their bread, but this time the piece was smaller still. As they walked into the forest, Hansel broke his up in his pocket, and kept stopping to drop a crumb on the ground. “Hansel, why do you keep stopping and looking back?” said the father. “Come along.” “I’m looking at my little pigeon sitting on the roof. It wants to say goodbye to me,” Hansel answered. “Fool!” said the woman. “That isn’t your pigeon. It’s the morning sun shining on the chimney.” But bit by bit, Hansel went on throwing every crumb onto the path.

The woman took the children even deeper into the forest, to a place they had never been in all their lives. Once more a big fire was lit, and the mother said: “Sit down here, children, and if you get tired you can sleep for a while. We’re going into the forest to chop wood. When we’ve finished this evening, we’ll come back and collect you.” At noon Gretel shared her bread with Hansel, since he had scattered his along the way. Then they fell asleep, and the evening went by, but nobody came for the poor children. They woke only when the night was pitch dark, and Hansel comforted his little sister. “Wait till the moon comes up, Gretel,” he said. “Then we’ll see the crumbs I dropped, and they’ll show us the way home.” When the moon rose, they set off, but there were no crumbs to be seen, because the thousands of birds that fly around the woods and fields had pecked up every one. Hansel said to Gretel, “We’ll find the way soon,” but they never did. They walked all night and the whole of the next day, from morning until evening, and still they couldn’t get out of the forest. They were very hungry, since all they had to eat was a few berries growing on the ground. And when they were so tired that their legs would not carry them any further, they lay down under a tree and fell asleep.

Three mornings had now passed since they left their father’s house. They started walking again, but they only went deeper into the forest, and unless help came soon, they would die of hunger and exhaustion. At midday they saw a beautiful snow-white bird perched on a branch. It sang so sweetly that they stopped and listened. When its song ended, it spread its wings and flew off ahead of them, and they followed it until they came to a little house. The bird landed on the roof, and as the children came closer they saw that the house was made of bread and covered with cakes, and that its windows were clear sugar. “Let’s get started on this,” said Hansel, “and have a proper meal. I’ll eat a piece of the roof, Gretel, and you can eat some of the window. It will taste sweet.” Hansel reached up and broke off a bit of the roof to see what it tasted like, while Gretel leaned against the window and nibbled at the panes. Then a soft voice called out from inside the room:

“Nibble, nibble, gnaw,
Who is nibbling at my little house?”
The children answered:

“The wind, the wind,
The child of heaven, the wind,”

and they carried on eating, not bothered in the least. Hansel liked the taste of the roof so much that he tore off a huge piece, and Gretel pushed out an entire round windowpane, sat down, and enjoyed it. All at once the door opened, and out crept a woman as old as the hills, leaning on crutches. Hansel and Gretel were so badly frightened that they dropped everything they were holding. The old woman only nodded her head and said, “Oh, dear children, who brought you here? Come inside and stay with me. No harm will come to you.” She took them both by the hand and led them into her little house. Then she put a good meal in front of them: milk and pancakes with sugar, apples, and nuts. Afterwards she made up two pretty little beds with clean white sheets, and Hansel and Gretel lay down in them and felt as if they were in heaven.

The old woman had only pretended to be kind. In truth she was a wicked witch who lay in wait for children, and she had built her little bread house just to lure them in. When a child fell into her hands, she killed it, cooked it and ate it, and for her that was a feast day. Witches have red eyes and can’t see far, but they have a sharp sense of smell, like animals, and know when people are near. As Hansel and Gretel came close to her house, she gave a nasty laugh and said with a sneer, “I’ve got them! They won’t get away from me this time!” She was up early in the morning, before the children woke, and when she saw the two of them asleep, looking so lovely with their plump rosy cheeks, she muttered to herself, “What a tasty bite that will be!” Then she grabbed Hansel with her bony hand, carried him to a little stable, and locked him in behind a barred door. He could scream all he liked; it did him no good. Then she went to Gretel, shook her awake, and shouted, “Get up, you lazy thing! Fetch some water and cook something good for your brother. He’s in the stable outside, and he’s going to be fattened up. When he’s fat, I’ll eat him.” Gretel began to cry bitterly, but it was no use. She had to do whatever the wicked witch told her.

So the finest food was cooked for poor Hansel, while Gretel got nothing but crab shells. Every morning the old woman crept out to the little stable and called, “Hansel, stick out your finger, so I can feel whether you’re getting fat.” But Hansel held out a small bone instead. The old woman had weak eyes and couldn’t see it. She thought it was Hansel’s finger, and she was amazed that he didn’t get any fatter. After four weeks had passed and Hansel was still thin, she lost patience and refused to wait any longer. “Now then, Gretel,” she shouted at the girl, “get moving and bring some water. Fat or thin, tomorrow I’ll kill Hansel and cook him.” Oh, how the poor little sister wept as she carried the water, and how the tears ran down her cheeks! “Dear God, please help us,” she cried. “If only the wild animals in the forest had eaten us, at least we would have died together.” “Save your whining,” said the old woman. “It won’t do you any good.”

Early in the morning, Gretel had to go out, hang the cauldron of water over the fire, and light it. “First we’ll bake,” said the old woman. “I’ve already heated the oven and kneaded the dough.” She shoved poor Gretel toward the oven, where flames were already leaping out. “Crawl in,” said the witch, “and check whether it’s hot enough for us to put the bread in.” Her plan was to shut the oven once Gretel was inside, and bake her in it, and then eat her too. But Gretel saw what she was up to, and said, “I don’t know how to do it. How do I get in?” “Stupid goose,” said the old woman. “The opening is big enough. Look, I could get in myself!” And she scrambled up and stuck her head into the oven. Then Gretel gave her a shove that sent her flying right inside, slammed the iron door, and slid the bolt across. Oh! The witch began to howl horribly, but Gretel ran off, and the godless witch burned to a miserable death.

Gretel ran to Hansel as fast as lightning, opened his little stable, and cried, “Hansel, we’re saved! The old witch is dead!” Hansel leaped out like a bird from a cage when the door is opened. How they cheered, and hugged, and danced around, and kissed each other! Now that they had nothing to fear from her, they went into the witch’s house, and in every corner stood chests full of pearls and jewels. “These are much better than pebbles!” said Hansel, and he stuffed his pockets with as much as they would hold. Gretel said, “I’ll take something home too,” and filled her apron to the top. “But now we have to go,” said Hansel, “so we can get out of the witch’s forest.”

After they had walked for two hours, they came to a wide stretch of water. “We can’t get across,” said Hansel. “I can’t see a plank or a bridge anywhere.” “There’s no ferry either,” Gretel answered, “but there’s a white duck swimming over there. If I ask her, she’ll help us across.” Then she called out:

“Little duck, little duck, do you see
Hansel and Gretel, who are waiting for you?
There is no plank and no bridge in sight,
Carry us over on your back so white.”

The duck swam over to them, and Hansel sat down on her back and told his sister to sit beside him. “No,” Gretel replied, “that would be too heavy for the little duck. She should take us across one at a time.” The kind little duck did just that. Once they were safely over and had walked on a little way, the forest began to look more and more familiar, and at last they saw their father’s house in the distance. Then they started to run, burst into the room, and threw their arms around their father’s neck. The man had not had one happy hour since he left the children in the forest, and the woman was dead. Gretel shook out her apron until pearls and precious stones rolled across the floor, and Hansel tossed down one handful after another from his pocket to add to them. All their worries were over, and they lived together in perfect happiness. My tale is done; see, a mouse is running by. Whoever catches it can make himself a big fur cap out of it.
